tagline: A city, an island, and a country
overview:
Singapore is a city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, one main island plus about 60 small ones, sitting almost on the equator. At roughly 710 km² it is smaller than New York City, and it has grown by about a quarter since independence by reclaiming land from the sea. Causeways and a bridge link it to Malaysia; Indonesia lies just across the strait.

About 6 million people live in Singapore, one of the most densely populated countries on Earth. Four languages are official: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil. English is the language of school and business, and Malay provides the national anthem.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic and has been governed by the same party since 1959. Its harbor is one of the busiest ports in the world, and in about sixty years the country went from a struggling trading post to one of the wealthiest places on the planet.
landAndNature: The island is low and flat; Bukit Timah Hill, at 164 meters, is the highest natural point, and its surrounding reserve holds a patch of original rainforest with long-tailed macaques, pangolins and flying lemurs. Being just north of the equator, Singapore is hot and humid all year, around 31°C most days, with sudden heavy downpours and thunder more than 150 days a year. The city calls itself a City in a Garden: trees line the expressways, and the Gardens by the Bay built vertical steel Supertrees planted with ferns and orchids. The Sungei Buloh wetlands attract migrating shorebirds, otters swim in the reservoirs and canals right through downtown, and the national flower is a hybrid orchid.
peopleAndCulture: Singapore's people are mainly of Chinese, Malay and Indian descent, and public holidays include Chinese New Year, Hari Raya Puasa, Deepavali and Christmas. Many people speak Singlish, a quick-fire English sprinkled with Malay and Chinese words and ending tags like lah. Food is a national obsession, eaten in hawker centers where dozens of stalls sell chicken rice, laksa, chili crab, char kway teow and roti prata for a few dollars; the hawker culture is on UNESCO's heritage list. About four in five people live in well-planned public housing blocks. Rules are strict and famously enforced: chewing gum cannot be sold, and littering brings heavy fines, which is part of why the city is so clean.
history: A port called Temasek stood here in the 1300s, and the name Singapura, Lion City, comes from a legend of a prince who saw a strange beast. Sir Stamford Raffles established a British trading post in 1819, and the free port drew merchants and workers from China, India and the Malay world, becoming one of Asia's busiest harbors. Japan captured Singapore in February 1942 in a shattering defeat for Britain and occupied it for three and a half years. After the war Singapore moved toward self-rule, joined Malaysia in 1963, and was expelled two years later, becoming an unwilling independent country on August 9, 1965. Under Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew it built housing, schools, industry and clean government, and living standards rose dramatically within a single generation.
funFacts: Singapore is one of only three surviving city-states in the world, along with Monaco and Vatican City.
The country has grown about 25 percent larger since the 1960s by filling in land along its coasts.
Selling chewing gum is banned, though gum prescribed by a dentist or pharmacist is allowed.
Changi Airport has a 40-meter indoor waterfall, and its terminals include gardens, slides and a cinema.
Singapore collects rainwater across two-thirds of the island and recycles wastewater into drinking water called NEWater.
